{{Short description|Mathematical object}}
{{Refimprove|date=December 2017}}

In [[mathematics]], an '''initial algebra''' is an [[initial object]] in the [[Category (mathematics)|category]] of [[F-algebra|{{mvar|F}}-algebras]] for a given [[endofunctor]] {{mvar|F}}. This initiality provides a general framework for [[mathematical induction|induction]] and [[recursion]]. 

== Examples ==

=== Functor {{math|1 + (−)}} ===

Consider the endofunctor {{math|1 + (−)}}, i.e. {{math|''F'' : '''Set''' → '''Set'''}} sending {{mvar|X}} to {{math|1 + ''X''}}, where {{math|1}} is a one-point ([[Singleton (mathematics)|singleton]]) [[Set (mathematics)|set]], a [[terminal object]] in the category. An algebra for this endofunctor is a set {{mvar|X}} (called the ''carrier'' of the algebra) together with a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] {{math|''f'' : (1 + ''X'') → ''X''}}. Defining such a function amounts to defining a point {{math|''x'' ∈ ''X''}} and a function {{math|''X'' → ''X''}}.
Define
:<math displaystyle="block">
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{zero} \colon 1 &\longrightarrow\mathbf{N} \\
  * &\longmapsto 0
\end{align}
</math> 
and
:<math displaystyle="block">
\begin{align}
  \operatorname{succ}\colon \mathbf{N}&\longrightarrow\mathbf{N} \\
  n &\longmapsto n + 1.
\end{align}
</math>
Then the set {{math|'''N'''}} of natural numbers together with the function {{math|[zero,succ]: 1 + '''N''' → '''N'''}} is an initial {{mvar|F}}-algebra. The initiality (the [[universal property]] for this case) is not hard to establish; the unique [[homomorphism]] to an arbitrary {{mvar|F}}-algebra {{math|(''A'', [''e'', ''f''])}}, for {{math|''e'': 1 → ''A''}} an element of {{mvar|A}} and {{math|''f'': ''A'' → ''A''}} a function on {{mvar|A}}, is the function sending the natural number {{mvar|n}} to {{math|''f<sup>n</sup>''(''e'')}}, that is, {{math|''f''(''f''(…(''f''(''e''))…))}}, the {{mvar|n}}-fold application of {{mvar|f}} to {{mvar|e}}.

The set of [[natural number]]s is the carrier of an initial algebra for this functor: the point is zero and the function is the [[successor function]].

=== Functor {{math|1 + N × (−)}} ===

For a second example, consider the endofunctor {{math|1 + '''N''' × (−)}} on the category of sets, where {{math|'''N'''}} is the set of natural numbers. An algebra for this endofunctor is a set {{mvar|X}} together with a function {{math|1 + '''N''' × ''X'' → ''X''}}. To define such a function, we need a point {{math|''x'' ∈ ''X''}} and a function {{math|'''N''' × ''X'' → ''X''}}. The set of finite [[List (computing)|list]]s of natural numbers is an initial algebra for this functor. The point is the empty list, and the function is [[cons]], taking a number and a finite list, and returning a new finite list with the number at the head.

In categories with binary [[coproduct]]s, the definitions just given are equivalent to the usual definitions of a [[natural number object]] and a [[list object]], respectively.

==Final coalgebra==
[[Duality (mathematics)|Dually]], a '''final coalgebra''' is a [[terminal object]] in the category of [[F-coalgebra|{{mvar|F}}-coalgebras]]. The finality provides a general framework for [[coinduction]] and [[corecursion]].

For example, using the same [[functor]] {{math|1 + (−)}} as before, a coalgebra is defined as a set {{mvar|X}} together with a function {{math|''f'' : ''X'' → (1 + ''X'')}}. Defining such a function amounts to defining a [[partial function]] {{math|''f''': ''X'' ⇸ ''X''}} whose [[Domain of a function|domain]] is formed by those <math>x \in X</math> for which {{math|''f''(''x'')}} does not belong to {{math|1}}. Having such a structure, we can define a chain of sets: {{math|''X''<sub>0</sub>}} being a subset of {{math|''X''}} on which {{math|''f''′}} is not defined, {{math|''X''<sub>1</sub>}} which elements map into {{math|''X''<sub>0</sub>}} by {{math|''f''′}}, {{math|''X''<sub>2</sub>}} which elements map into {{math|''X''<sub>1</sub>}} by {{math|''f''′}}, etc., and {{math|''X''<sub>''ω''</sub>}} containing the remaining elements of {{mvar|X}}. With this in view, the set <math>\mathbf{N} \cup \{\omega\}</math>, consisting of the set of natural numbers extended with a new element {{mvar|ω}}, is the carrier of the final coalgebra, where <math>f'</math> is the predecessor function (the [[Inverse function|inverse]] of the successor function) on the positive naturals, but acts like the [[Identity function|identity]] on the new element {{mvar|ω}}: {{math|1=''f''(''n'' + 1) = ''n''}}, {{math|1=''f''(''ω'') = ''ω''}}. This set <math>\mathbf{N} \cup \{\omega\}</math> that is the carrier of the final coalgebra of {{math|1 + (−)}} is known as the set of conatural numbers.

For a second example, consider the same functor {{math|1 + '''N''' × (−)}} as before. In this case the carrier of the final coalgebra consists of all lists of natural numbers, finite as well as [[Infinite list|infinite]]. The operations are a test function testing whether a list is empty, and a deconstruction function defined on non-empty lists returning a pair consisting of the head and the tail of the input list.

== Theorems ==
* Initial algebras are minimal (i.e., have no proper subalgebra).
* Final coalgebras are [[Simple algebra|simple]] (i.e., have no proper quotients).

== Use in computer science ==

Various finite [[data structures]] used in [[Mathematical programming|programming]], such as [[List (computing)|list]]s and [[tree (data structure)|tree]]s, can be obtained as initial algebras of specific endofunctors.
While there may be several initial algebras for a given endofunctor, they are [[unique (mathematics)|unique]] [[up to]] [[isomorphism]], which informally means that the "observable" properties of a data structure can be adequately captured by defining it as an initial algebra.

To obtain the [[Data type|type]] {{math|List(''A'')}} of lists whose elements are members of set {{mvar|A}}, consider that the list-forming operations are:

*<math>\mathrm{nil}\colon 1 \to \mathrm{List}(A)</math>
*<math>\mathrm{cons}\colon A \times \mathrm{List}(A) \to \mathrm{List}(A)</math>

Combined into one function, they give:

*<math>[\mathrm{nil},\mathrm{cons}]\colon (1 + A \times \mathrm{List}(A))\to \mathrm{List}(A),</math>

which makes this an {{mvar|F}}-algebra for the endofunctor {{mvar|F}} sending {{mvar|X}} to {{math|1 + (''A'' × ''X'')}}. It is, in fact, ''the'' initial {{mvar|F}}-algebra. Initiality is established by the function known as ''[[Fold (higher-order function)|foldr]]'' in [[functional programming|functional]] [[programming language]]s such as [[Haskell (programming language)|Haskell]] and [[ML programming language|ML]].

Likewise, [[binary tree]]s with elements at the leaves can be obtained as the initial algebra

*<math>[\mathrm{tip},\mathrm{join}]\colon A + (\mathrm{Tree}(A) \times \mathrm{Tree}(A)) \to \mathrm{Tree}(A).</math>

Types obtained this way are known as [[algebraic data type]]s.

Types defined by using [[least fixed point]] construct with functor {{mvar|F}} can be regarded as an initial {{mvar|F}}-algebra, provided that [[parametricity]] holds for the type.<ref name=free-rectypes>Philip Wadler: [http://homepages.inf.ed.ac.uk/wadler/papers/free-rectypes/free-rectypes.txt Recursive types for free!] University of Glasgow, July 1990. Draft.</ref>

In a dual way, similar relationship exists between notions of [[greatest fixed point]] and terminal {{mvar|F}}-coalgebra, with applications to [[coinductive]] types.  These can be used for allowing [[Actual infinity|potentially infinite]] objects while maintaining [[Normalization property (lambda-calculus)|strong normalization property]].<ref name=free-rectypes/> In the strongly normalizing (each program terminates) Charity programming language, coinductive data types can be used for achieving surprising results, e.g. defining [[Lookup table|lookup]] constructs to implement such [[Computability theory (computer science)|“strong”]] functions like the [[Ackermann function]].<ref>[[Robin Cockett]]: Charitable Thoughts ([http://pll.cpsc.ucalgary.ca/charity1/download/literature/papers_and_reports/charitable.ps.gz ps.gz])</ref>
